label: PART VI
title: Building Confidence While Changing Code
lead: Use a risk-shaped test portfolio and deployment-safe migration techniques instead of betting on one giant rewrite.

chapters.title: Testing strategy and modern change workflows
chapters.intro: Tests are a risk-control portfolio and a design feedback system. The goal is confidence at useful speed, not maximum test count.

concepts.title: Testing Strategy
concepts.definition: A testing strategy chooses test scope according to risk and boundary: fast tests for rules, focused integration tests for adapters, contract tests for independently changing parties, and a small number of end-to-end journeys.
concepts.look_for: For each important failure, choose the cheapest reliable test that includes the boundary capable of causing it rather than following a fixed test-count quota.
concepts.python_expanded:
def test_empty_order_cannot_be_placed():
    order = Order()

    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        order.place()


async def test_saved_order_can_be_loaded_from_real_database(database_order_store, order):
    await database_order_store.save(order)

    loaded = await database_order_store.load(order.id)

    assert loaded.total == order.total
concepts.walkthrough: The first test exercises `Order.Place` entirely in memory. That is the lowest useful boundary for the rule that an empty order cannot be placed, so database setup would add cost without confidence. The second test deliberately uses `databaseOrderStore` twice because the risk is mapping and persistence: saving and loading through the real adapter proves more than a mock can. Together they illustrate strategy as risk allocation, not as a contest to maximize unit tests. Contract tests would cover an independently released provider's request and response agreement; end-to-end tests would reserve their slower deployed setup for a critical journey spanning several components. Test shape should follow where uncertainty lives. A test pyramid is a useful economic tendency - many cheap tests, fewer costly ones - but not a universal ratio. A UI-heavy product or data pipeline may need a different portfolio.
concepts.caution: Mocks at every boundary can create a fast suite that verifies only your assumptions. Conversely, too many end-to-end tests produce slow, flaky feedback with poor diagnosis. Review the mix against actual escaped failures.
concepts.related: Unit Test; Integration Test; Contract Test; End-to-End Test

concepts.title: Unit Tests and Arrange-Act-Assert
concepts.definition: A unit test verifies one behavior through a small, deterministic boundary. Arrange-Act-Assert separates relevant setup, one meaningful action, and observations of the outcome.
concepts.look_for: Name the scenario and expected result, keep inputs purposeful, and assert public behavior rather than private method calls or incidental object layout.
concepts.python_expanded:
def test_premium_customer_receives_ten_percent_discount():
    # Arrange
    customer = Customer(is_premium=True)
    subtotal = Decimal("100")

    # Act
    discounted_total = customer.calculate_discounted_total(subtotal)

    # Assert
    assert discounted_total == Decimal("90")
concepts.walkthrough: The test name states the scenario and promised outcome. Arrangement creates a premium `Customer` and a `subtotal` of 100. The single act calls `CalculateDiscountedTotal`; the assertion observes the returned total of 90. Those divisions make the failure easy to interpret and keep setup mechanics from being confused with behavior. The unit is the small public boundary under test, not necessarily one class or one method in isolation. Several collaborating value objects may still form a fast deterministic unit. Likewise, one assertion is not a law: several assertions can describe one coherent outcome, such as a returned value and a domain event. Trouble begins when one test performs several unrelated actions or verifies private calls, because harmless refactoring then looks like broken behavior. Arrange-Act-Assert is a reading aid, not a demand for comments when spacing and naming already make the phases obvious.
concepts.caution: Tests that mirror implementation details make structural improvement expensive. Control time, randomness, and external I/O at the boundary, but avoid mocking collaborators whose real behavior is cheap and essential to the rule.

concepts.title: Integration, Contract, and End-to-End Tests
concepts.definition: Integration tests exercise real technical boundaries, contract tests verify agreements between independently changing parties, and end-to-end tests traverse a critical journey through the deployed system shape.
concepts.look_for: Choose the narrowest scope that includes the failure-prone boundary; reserve end-to-end setup for journeys whose cross-system wiring is itself important.
concepts.python_expanded:
async def test_order_round_trips_through_real_database(sql_order_store):
    # Arrange
    order = order_samples.placed_order()

    # Act
    await sql_order_store.save(order)
    loaded = await sql_order_store.load(order.id)

    # Assert
    assert loaded is not None
    assert loaded.total == order.total
    assert loaded.status == order.status


# A separate provider contract test verifies status code and JSON schema.
# A small deployed test verifies that a customer can complete checkout.
concepts.walkthrough: The round-trip test includes the real `sqlOrderStore` and database because mapping, schema, transactions, and query behavior are the risks being checked. It remains narrower than an end-to-end test: no browser, payment provider, or deployed checkout workflow is required. A provider contract test would focus on a service agreement such as response status, field names, types, and compatibility with a consumer's expectations; it may run separately in both delivery pipelines. An end-to-end test would cross the deployed entry point and major dependencies to confirm that a customer can complete checkout. These labels describe boundaries, not just speed. A test using five real in-memory domain objects can still be a unit test, while a test of one repository against a real database is an integration test. Mocks cannot prove a boundary agrees with reality when the mock was written from the same mistaken assumption as the client.
concepts.caution: Broad tests are expensive to prepare, diagnose, and stabilize. Keep test data isolated, make boundary versions explicit, and use focused integration tests to locate failures before adding another end-to-end scenario.

concepts.title: Test Doubles: Fakes, Stubs, Spies, and Mocks
concepts.definition: Test doubles replace collaborators during a test: fakes have lightweight working behavior, stubs return prepared answers, spies record calls, and mocks encode interaction expectations.
concepts.look_for: Choose the least behaviorally coupled double that proves the result. Prefer state or returned values unless the interaction itself is the external obligation.
concepts.walkthrough: `FakeClock` is a small working implementation of `IClock`: its `UtcNow` can be read and changed, so the test controls time without waiting or patching a global clock. `TokenService` receives the fake through the same boundary used by production, and the assertion checks the observable expiration decision. A stub would instead return one prepared response from a dependency. A spy would record calls so the test could inspect them afterward. A mock usually combines configured answers with expectations such as 'send exactly once.' Libraries blur these names, but the conceptual distinction matters because interaction assertions couple a test to how work is performed. When the outcome is enough, a fake or stub usually survives refactoring better. Use a spy or mock when the call itself is the obligation - for example, writing an audit record or publishing a message.
concepts.caution: Over-mocking turns call order and internal decomposition into a second implementation that tests must maintain. Do not fake the boundary whose real compatibility you need to establish; use an integration or contract test there.
concepts.related: Dependency Injection; London and Classical TDD; Integration Test

concepts.title: Characterization and Golden-Master Tests
concepts.definition: A characterization test records behavior that uncertain legacy code exhibits today. A golden-master or approval test compares a larger output with a reviewed reference artifact.
concepts.look_for: Use them to establish a safety net before changing code whose intended rules are unknown; replace broad snapshots with focused assertions as understanding improves.
concepts.python_expanded:
def test_legacy_statement_matches_reviewed_output():
    # Arrange
    sample_order = statement_samples.order_with_discount_and_tax()
    approved_path = Path("approved-statement.txt")
    approved = approved_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

    # Act
    actual = legacy_statement_renderer.render(sample_order)

    # Assert
    assert actual == approved
concepts.walkthrough: The test does not claim that `legacyStatementRenderer.Render` is correct according to a newly written specification. It records that, for `sampleOrder`, the renderer currently produces the reviewed contents of `approved-statement.txt`. That distinction makes it a characterization test and gives a refactoring a regression alarm before anyone fully understands the old rules. Because the approved value is a whole statement rather than a few focused facts, it is also a golden-master or approval-style test. The fixture deliberately includes discount and tax so the captured path is meaningful. When the output changes, a reviewer must decide whether the diff reveals a regression, an intentional correction, or irrelevant formatting. As rules become known, focused tests such as 'tax is rounded once at the statement total' should supplement or replace portions of the broad snapshot. A golden master protects observed behavior; it does not certify that observed behavior was ever desirable.
concepts.caution: A snapshot can preserve bugs and make harmless timestamps, ordering, or whitespace look significant. Normalize only truly nondeterministic fields, review every approval diff, and keep fixtures small enough to understand.
concepts.related: Approval Testing; Snapshot Testing; Behavior-Preserving Change

concepts.title: Property-Based Testing
concepts.definition: Property-based testing states a general law and asks a framework to generate many inputs, reporting and shrinking failures toward a small counterexample.
concepts.look_for: Use it for parsers, serializers, collections, arithmetic, transformations, and state machines with laws that hold over broad input spaces.
concepts.walkthrough: The round-trip property says `Decode(Encode(text))` must equal `text` for every supported string, not just 'hello.' A property framework supplies empty strings, Unicode, long inputs, and combinations the author may not think to enumerate. When it finds a failure, shrinking searches for a smaller string that still fails, often revealing the rule that was violated. The sorting property checks two independent consequences: output count is preserved and adjacent values are ordered. A complete sorting property would also verify the same multiset of elements, because an implementation that returns repeated zeros could satisfy the two shown assertions for some inputs. This illustrates the central discipline: properties must express domain laws independently of the algorithm. Generated examples complement carefully chosen examples; they do not replace scenarios whose business significance depends on named cases, external integrations, or exact messages.
concepts.caution: Weak or tautological properties create impressive input counts without useful assurance. Control generator domains, reproduce failures with recorded seeds, and remember that shrinking can obscure a failure that depends on history or timing.

concepts.title: Test-Driven Development
concepts.definition: Test-Driven Development cycles through a failing behavioral example, the smallest implementation that passes, and design improvement while the suite remains green.
concepts.look_for: Use Red-Green-Refactor when concrete examples can guide a useful API; run a technical spike first when the main uncertainty is feasibility or unfamiliar infrastructure.
concepts.python_expanded:
# RED: this test fails because add does not reject zero yet.
def test_add_rejects_zero_quantity():
    order = Order()

    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        order.add(product, 0)


# GREEN: add the smallest rule to Order.add.
def add(self, product, quantity):
    if quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError("quantity must be positive")
    self._lines.append(OrderLine(product, quantity))


# REFACTOR: improve names or move the rule while all tests stay green.
concepts.walkthrough: The red test names one missing behavior: `Order.Add` must reject a quantity of zero. It is valuable that the test fails for the expected reason before implementation; an already-green test may not exercise the gap. The green version adds the smallest complete rule, including all nonpositive quantities, and avoids unrelated redesign. Refactoring then improves names or moves responsibility while this and neighboring tests protect behavior. The C# expanded test uses an anonymous delegate with braces because `Assert.Throws` needs deferred behavior, not the result of calling `Add`. The shorthand lambda means the same thing: its target type is `Action`, it returns no value, and it captures `order` and `product`. TDD is a feedback and design practice, not a guarantee of good architecture or exhaustive coverage. Integration risks, migration plans, and system constraints still require deliberate design beyond the local cycle.
concepts.caution: TDD can optimize a local API while missing system-level failure modes. Keep cycles small, but periodically step back to review architecture, boundary tests, performance, security, and whether the tests assert useful behavior.

concepts.title: Modern Refactoring Workflow
concepts.definition: A modern refactoring workflow establishes fast feedback, applies one behavior-preserving transformation, runs focused checks, reviews the diff, and records a small coherent change.
concepts.look_for: Separate structural changes from feature changes when practical so reviewers can verify intent, failures are attributable, and history remains easy to bisect.
concepts.csharp_shorthand:
public static decimal CalculateDiscount(decimal subtotal) =>
    subtotal >= 100m ? 10m : 0m;
concepts.python_shorthand:
def calculate_discount(subtotal):
    return Decimal("10") if subtotal >= Decimal("100") else Decimal("0")
concepts.walkthrough: `before` captures the current observable result of `LegacyTotal`. The next step extracts `CalculateDiscount` without changing the threshold or amount. `RefactoredTotal` is then compared with the saved result before the legacy path disappears. That side-by-side check is temporary scaffolding; the durable characterization and domain tests remain after migration. An IDE can safely perform mechanical work such as renaming or extracting a method, while a developer must still decide whether discount policy belongs in this function. The shorthand shows how an expression-bodied member and conditional expression compress the same two return paths after their meaning is understood. The workflow's small steps narrow the search space when a check fails, make diffs reviewable, and enable frequent commits. Compiler success is useful feedback but does not establish runtime behavior, data compatibility, or performance; select checks according to the risk of the particular change.
concepts.caution: A giant 'cleanup' pull request defeats the safety and review benefits even if every edit is individually defensible. Avoid mixing renames, formatting, dependency upgrades, and behavior changes in one opaque diff.
concepts.related: Characterization Test; Behavior-Preserving Change; Preparatory Refactoring

concepts.title: Branch by Abstraction and Strangler Fig
concepts.definition: Branch by Abstraction puts old and new implementations behind one seam for gradual replacement. Strangler Fig routes slices of a legacy system to a new implementation until the old path can be retired.
concepts.look_for: Use them when a migration cannot fit safely in one deployment and old and new behavior must coexist under controlled routing.
concepts.walkthrough: Both invoice engines implement `IInvoiceEngine`, and callers use only `RoutingInvoiceEngine.Create`. The routing seam chooses `_newEngine` for an enabled customer cohort and `_legacyEngine` otherwise. That is Branch by Abstraction: the codebase can introduce the interface, adapt the legacy implementation, build the replacement, and shift traffic across several releasable steps. If the same technique sits at an HTTP gateway and replaces whole endpoint slices, it is commonly described as a Strangler Fig migration. The feature flag is routing machinery, not the migration strategy by itself. Instrumenting results from both paths can reveal correctness and performance before full cutover. The abstraction must represent stable invoice behavior rather than the quirks of either engine, or the replacement remains coupled to legacy design. Completion includes removing the router, flag, adapter, and old implementation once evidence and rollback windows permit.
concepts.caution: Coexistence creates duplicate logic, compatibility paths, and operational ambiguity. Assign an owner, success metrics, rollback criteria, and a deletion date so the temporary branch does not become permanent architecture.
concepts.related: Feature Toggle; Parallel Change; Anti-Corruption Layer

concepts.title: Expand-Contract Migration and Progressive Delivery
concepts.definition: Expand-Contract first makes old and new representations compatible, migrates producers, consumers, and data, then removes the old form. Progressive delivery limits exposure while evidence accumulates.
concepts.look_for: Use it when database columns, message schemas, APIs, or algorithms cannot change atomically across every deployed consumer.
concepts.csharp_shorthand:
public static string GetDisplayName(CustomerRow row) =>
    row.DisplayName ?? $"{row.FirstName} {row.LastName}".Trim();
concepts.python_shorthand:
def get_display_name(row):
    return row.display_name or f"{row.first_name} {row.last_name}".strip()
concepts.walkthrough: `GetDisplayName` is the expansion seam: a newly deployed reader understands `DisplayName` but still falls back to `FirstName` and `LastName`. Writers can begin populating the new field, a backfill can migrate existing rows, and telemetry can show whether any fallback reads remain. Only after every consumer understands the new representation does the contract phase remove the old columns and compatibility branch. That ordering avoids a deployment in which an old reader encounters data it cannot understand. Progressive delivery adds controlled exposure - perhaps enabling the new writer for staff, then 5%, then 50% - and supplies pause or rollback points. The shorthand versions are readable after the compatibility rule is clear, but note that Python's `or` also falls back for an empty string, while C# `??` falls back only for `null`; choose semantics deliberately. Expand-Contract governs compatibility; feature flags govern exposure.
concepts.caution: Compatibility code and flags are temporary inventory. Give each an owner and removal condition, monitor mixed-version behavior, and never contract until deployed consumers and retained messages can no longer require the old form.
concepts.related: Parallel Change; Feature Toggle; Schema Evolution
